reading.body:
Verizon's AI lobbying footprint is five LDA filings, worked by a roster of sixteen lobbyists and naming six bills.

The pattern is concentration at the top and a long tail below it. Five lobbyists appear on all five filings, six more appear on four, and five appear on just one. That is what a standing account looks like rather than a one-off push: a core team carries the file and others are added for particular bills or particular meetings. The bills named are all from 2025 or later, three in the Senate and three in the House, which places the activity in the current Congress rather than in a historical record.

For AI specifically, this is telecom infrastructure money watching AI rules, not a model developer or a data center builder. Verizon's interest in AI legislation runs through the network and the services layered on it, so its lobbying is a signal about how AI regulation touches carriers, not about how it touches compute supply. The filings record that AI was a subject lobbied on. They do not record what Verizon argued, and the source data here does not say which of the six bills were supported, opposed, or merely monitored.

What this does not cover is equally important. There is no spending figure, no agency or chamber targeted, no text of any filing, and no indication of whether these five filings are all of Verizon's AI lobbying or only the ones this dataset holds. Sixteen names on a client page is a measure of disclosure activity, not of influence.
